candidateRoutes: continue incremental improvement of atmospheric engines
separate condensation from the working cylinder while keeping the cylinder hot
after efficiency improvement, convert reciprocating motion into rotary factory power
continue relying on water power where geography allowed
complements: Matthew Boulton's capital, manufactory and commercial organization
accurately bored cylinders and improving machine-tool capability
on-site construction and skilled installation because engines were large and non-modular
financing/business arrangements tied to coal savings rather than simple upfront machine sale
decisiveTests: The 1769 patent explicitly framed the invention as a method for reducing steam and fuel consumption.
Science Museum reconstruction reports roughly two-thirds lower coal consumption relative to earlier engines, sufficient to widen viable use beyond mines.
Boulton's Soho installation and later rotative engines demonstrated sustained factory work rather than only model performance.
record.diffusionAndScaling: Watt's condenser was patented in 1769, but transforming it into a reliable industrial product took years. Boulton & Watt's engines remained expensive and difficult to acquire/install; diffusion depended on factory economics, complementary precision and commercialization. Later steam designs continued to improve after Watt.
record.externalitiesAndCorrections: Coal-powered steam relaxed geographic power constraints but deepened fossil-fuel dependence. This consequence was outside the local eighteenth-century engineering objective and became visible only at much larger temporal and system scales.
observationsAndInstruments: Watt's work on a model engine focused attention on the large heat loss caused by repeatedly cooling the cylinder.
The separate condenser physically separated steam condensation from the hot cylinder.
Surviving models and full-size Boulton & Watt rotative engines provide material evidence of the transition from concept to industrial machine.
record.preExistingWorldModel: Atmospheric steam engines were established pumping machines. Their cylinder was repeatedly heated by incoming steam and cooled by injected water for condensation, so the same cylinder alternated between incompatible thermal roles. Rotary factory machinery was still commonly driven by water power.
record.pressure: Newcomen-type atmospheric engines could pump mines but consumed so much coal that their economics strongly favored coalfield locations. A broader industrial prime mover required materially lower fuel consumption and eventually useful rotary output.
rivalsAndFailures: Newcomen atmospheric engines remained useful where coal was cheap and pumping was the dominant task.
Water power remained cheaper and attractive at good sites; steam's later diffusion was not an instantaneous replacement.
Watt's first financial backer John Roebuck failed financially, delaying the path from invention to commercial system.
record.secondOrderEffects: Efficient steam power expanded feasible factory location and demand for precision engineering, machine tools, boilers, controls and specialist engineering services. It became a platform upon which later industrial innovations accumulated.
record.sourceNativeSummary: Watt did not invent steam power from zero. He attacked a specific thermodynamic/economic defect in an existing atmospheric-engine world, and the famous separate condenser became historically consequential only after commercialization, precision manufacturing, rotary mechanisms, skilled installation and customer economics made it a repeatable industrial system.
record.standardsAndInstitutions: Patent protection, Boulton & Watt's partnership, customer contracts and the emerging mechanical-engineering trade all shaped selection and diffusion. The product was partly sold as verified fuel saving rather than a standardized interchangeable machine.
record.technicalOrScientificTransition: Steam power changed from an extremely fuel-hungry mine-pumping technology toward a more efficient, commercially engineered prime mover that could be coupled to factory machinery. The transition required several later mechanical changes in addition to the separate condenser, including rotary transmission and control mechanisms.
record.title: From atmospheric mine pumping to Watt efficient rotative factory power

record.sourceNativeSummary: By 1799 Cayley separated lift, propulsion and control in the fixed-wing aircraft concept and by 1804 flew a model glider, but engines/material/control capabilities adequate for powered flight were missing. The representation was useful decades before the full intervention path became tractable.
record.title: Cayley fixed-wing aerodynamic decomposition

candidateRoutes: wet-chemical isolation/analysis only
qualitative flame-color observation
spectroscope with narrow slit/prism and comparison scale
treat solar dark lines as purely optical phenomena versus chemical signatures
complements: optical line tables and instrument makers
decisiveTests: Candidate elements had to show characteristic repeatable line patterns across samples/flames.
Unknown spectral lines had to persist after known elements were excluded before supporting a new-element claim.
Coincidence between laboratory element spectra and solar/stellar lines tested whether remote composition could be inferred rather than directly sampled.
Independent instrument makers/observers had to reproduce line positions and identifications.
record.diffusionAndScaling: Spectral analysis spread rapidly across chemistry and astronomy during the 1860s and contributed to discovery of additional elements and physical astronomy.
record.externalitiesAndCorrections: No dominant direct HD2 externality; the main consequence is expansion of observable reality and discovery capability.
observationsAndInstruments: Bunsen and Kirchhoff built a practical spectroscope around 1859 that resolved characteristic line patterns rather than gross color.
They used spectral lines to discover cesium and rubidium in 1860, demonstrating that the instrument could reveal previously unknown elements rather than merely identify known substances.
Kirchhoff linked bright emission and dark solar absorption lines, enabling chemical inference about the Sun and stars.
The same instrument class rapidly spread into chemical and astronomical observation, creating a shared representation across otherwise inaccessible objects.
record.preExistingWorldModel: Prism spectra and Fraunhofer solar lines were known, and Bunsen's burner enabled cleaner flame observations. The causal link between characteristic emission/absorption lines, terrestrial elements and solar/stellar composition had not yet become a general analytical method.
record.pressure: Chemists needed ways to identify substances at very low concentrations and astronomers lacked direct access to celestial materials. Visible flame colors were known but subjective; a more discriminating representation of light could turn color into repeatable chemical evidence.
rivalsAndFailures: Ordinary flame color was faster but insufficiently discriminating for close mixtures/new elements.
Wet chemistry remained essential for isolation/confirmation and did not become obsolete.
Spectral coincidence could be misassigned without adequate calibration/reference data; instrument interpretation, not only possession, mattered.
record.secondOrderEffects: Spectroscopy became a general scientific sensing platform, eventually enabling atomic physics, astrophysics and remote sensing.
record.sourceNativeSummary: Spectroscopy is a clean case where a better observation representation changed the reachable research frontier. The spectroscope did not merely measure an existing chemical answer more precisely; it revealed unknown elements and made remote celestial composition empirically addressable.
record.standardsAndInstitutions: Instrument makers, laboratory reference substances and shared published spectra made observations comparable. The method's cross-laboratory value depended on stable line identities rather than one observer's color description.
record.technicalOrScientificTransition: A measurement instrument transformed emitted/absorbed light into a chemical identity representation. It created an observation channel for objects that could not be physically sampled and directly generated new discoveries.
record.title: Spectroscopy as discovery instrument: Bunsen–Kirchhoff chemical spectra to celestial composition

record.sourceNativeSummary: Great Eastern pushed iron steamship size, capacity and long-range engineering far beyond contemporary commercial practice. The ship proved many scale capabilities but its intended passenger/commercial model struggled; later it found a very different high-value role as a cable-laying platform.
record.title: Great Eastern: extreme-scale steamship engineering without sustainable original commercial model

candidateRoutes: continue cathode-ray characterization only
trace the unexpected penetrating radiation with screens/photographic plates/absorbers
immediately exploit shadow imaging for medicine
defer practical use until physical ontology is settled
use empirical exposure constraints and shielding as injuries accumulate
decisiveTests: The anomaly had to persist under controlled changes of shielding/absorber geometry to establish radiation beyond ordinary visible light/cathode rays.
Photographic/screen contrast had to reveal hidden structure reproducibly enough for diagnosis.
Biological injury had to track exposure strongly enough to distinguish radiation hazard from unrelated chemical/electrical effects.
Practical safety recommendations had to reduce exposure despite incomplete mechanism/dosimetry.
record.diffusionAndScaling: X-ray imaging spread internationally within months into hospitals, surgery and military medicine; increasing use multiplied both diagnostic value and occupational/patient exposure.
record.externalitiesAndCorrections: The same radiation producing diagnostic value could injure operators/patients; delayed injury made hazard learning slower than utility diffusion. Safety became a separate objective requiring shielding, time/distance constraints and later measurement standards.
observationsAndInstruments: In November 1895 Röntgen noticed a nearby fluorescent screen glow during discharge-tube experiments despite shielding; he varied intervening materials and recorded penetrating shadows photographically.
Within weeks the skeletal image of a hand made the capability legible; medical imaging of fractures followed by January 1896 even though the rays' nature was unknown.
The extremely rapid research/adoption wave produced hundreds of papers and many medical/experimental uses in 1896.
Burns, dermatitis, hair loss and eye irritation appeared within months among experimenters/operators; early users did not initially understand the causal hazard.

Protection practices gradually emerged through shorter exposure, distance, filtration/shielding and professional warnings; the German Roentgen Society issued formal protection recommendations in 1913 while unified dose measurement remained immature.
record.preExistingWorldModel: Cathode rays and discharge tubes were active experimental subjects. Röntgen did not begin with a medical-imaging hypothesis; a fluorescent screen glowing outside the expected cathode-ray path became the anomaly. The physical nature of X-rays was not settled when medical value became obvious.
record.pressure: Cathode-ray experiments unexpectedly revealed penetrating radiation that could image hidden internal structures. The immediate research frontier split: characterize a new physical phenomenon, exploit its diagnostic utility, and learn its biological hazards—none of which had to wait for the others to be theoretically complete.
rivalsAndFailures: The discovery was not produced by a preselected medical-imaging route, challenging planned-question-only accounts of scientific progress.
Rapid useful adoption coexisted with ignorance of mechanism and cumulative dose.
Immediate medical success did not imply net-safe operation; operators were injured while producing useful images.
Early self-experiment and anecdotal injury reports were informative but not yet a standardized dose model.
Later safety correction should not retroactively turn the initial sensing capability into a failed discovery.
record.secondOrderEffects: X-rays opened radiology and non-destructive internal observation, while also generating radiation protection/dosimetry as new scientific/engineering domains.
record.sourceNativeSummary: X-rays are a frozen anti-case against a doctrine that valuable research must begin with a correctly framed discriminating question or wait for correct ontology. The anomaly was noticed first, utility appeared almost immediately, physical explanation lagged, and safety evidence lagged differently again. Progress was real but multi-axis and asynchronous.
record.standardsAndInstitutions: Medical societies and later radiological organizations developed professional protection guidance before comprehensive governmental radiation regulation. Instrument manufacturers and users initially held much local safety responsibility.
record.technicalOrScientificTransition: A serendipitous observation created a new sensing channel whose practical value outran physical ontology and safety theory. Discovery, application and risk correction therefore advanced asynchronously rather than along a clean theory→validation→deployment sequence.
record.title: X-rays: serendipitous discovery, rapid medical diffusion and radiation-safety correction before mechanism settled

candidateRoutes: continue break-bulk cargo with incremental port mechanization
truck trailers carried on ships
detachable standardized containers moved among truck/ship/rail
carrier-specific proprietary container sizes
purpose-built container ships/terminals with high-capacity cranes
decisiveTests: End-to-end cost/time had to include terminal, crane, ship utilization and inland handling rather than box fabrication cost.
A container system had to survive repeated handling and transfer across modes.
Interoperability standards had to be adopted widely enough that terminals, chassis and ships could share equipment investment.
record.diffusionAndScaling: By the late 1960s standardized containers and specialized ships/terminals were spreading across major international routes, setting up the later global container network.
record.externalitiesAndCorrections: Containerization reduced some port labor and reshaped waterfront geography; it also enabled much larger global freight volumes whose environmental/security consequences grew later.
observationsAndInstruments: The converted Ideal-X sailed in 1956 carrying 58 trailer bodies/containers, demonstrating rapid shipboard intermodal transfer.
Sea-Land and Matson pursued different early container routes and terminal investments.
Container economics depended on high crane productivity and redesigned ports/ships rather than the metal box alone.
ISO Technical Committee 104, created in 1961, coordinated dimensions, corner fittings, testing, handling and marking; first international freight-container standards were published in the 1960s.
Standardization enabled equipment and containers from different firms/countries to interoperate, reducing the risk of proprietary lock-in.
record.preExistingWorldModel: Boxes and specialized cargo containers existed before McLean, and trucking/rail/shipping were established systems. The unresolved issue was whether standardized large containers plus purpose-built handling could beat break-bulk across an entire intermodal route.
record.pressure: Break-bulk freight required repeated hand loading/unloading, causing high labor cost, delay, damage and theft at ports. A reusable cargo box could reduce handling only if ships, cranes, trucks, ports and competing carriers coordinated around interoperable dimensions and procedures.
rivalsAndFailures: Early carriers used incompatible sizes and practices, so local success could have fragmented into proprietary systems.
The container did not eliminate cargo handling; it moved work into packing/unpacking, terminal scheduling and capital-intensive crane/yard operations.
Labor displacement/conflict was a system consequence rather than a failure of box engineering.
record.secondOrderEffects: Standardized intermodal freight sharply reduced coordination/handling cost and expanded the feasible scale and geographic reach of later supply chains.
record.sourceNativeSummary: The HD5 container trajectory shows why a simple artifact can be misleading: the steel box mattered because dimensions, corner fittings, cranes, ships, terminals and inland modes converged enough to make the box a reusable coordination substrate.
record.standardsAndInstitutions: Shipping firms, port authorities, trucking/rail firms, labor organizations, ISO TC104, national standards bodies and customs/regulatory agencies all had to align partially.
record.technicalOrScientificTransition: Containerization shifted freight from labor-intensive piece handling to a standardized intermodal unit embedded in redesigned terminals, ships and scheduling. The key object was a coordinated logistics system, not a container artifact.
record.title: Containerization from shipboard experiment to standardized intermodal freight system

record.sourceNativeSummary: The 1960 Scribner shunt enabled repeated vascular access, converting dialysis from an acute/one-off intervention into a chronic treatment possibility and leading to outpatient dialysis centers.
record.title: Scribner shunt and chronic hemodialysis as a durable treatment system

candidateRoutes: ammonia molecular-beam maser
solid-state/magnetic masers
parallel Basov-Prokhorov quantum-amplifier schemes
optical-maser/laser resonator proposals
ruby solid-state laser
gas lasers such as helium-neon
conventional incoherent lamps/radio-frequency sources for measurement/communication
decisiveTests: A maser had to produce coherent microwave amplification/oscillation from population inversion, not only satisfy a theoretical transition condition.
Optical schemes had to overcome pumping, gain and cavity-loss constraints to reach net stimulated emission.
Different media/pumping routes had to demonstrate materially useful wavelength, power, continuous/pulsed operation and stability.
record.diffusionAndScaling: During the 1960s lasers proliferated into spectroscopy, metrology, ranging, medicine and research instrumentation; large communication/electronics markets matured later.
record.externalitiesAndCorrections: High-intensity optical radiation created eye/safety hazards and military applications; standards and safety controls developed alongside wider use.
observationsAndInstruments: Townes and collaborators built an ammonia maser in the early 1950s, demonstrating stimulated-emission microwave amplification/oscillation.
Basov and Prokhorov independently developed related maser/quantum-electronics theory and methods in the Soviet Union.
Schawlow and Townes described optical-maser conditions in 1958, translating the principle toward optical resonators.
Theodore Maiman operated a pulsed ruby laser in 1960, while helium-neon and other laser types quickly followed.
Laser coherence/intensity opened new spectroscopy, ranging, communication and measurement experiments whose value was not reducible to the first device architecture.
record.preExistingWorldModel: Einstein’s stimulated-emission concept existed, while microwave spectroscopy and resonant cavities were mature enough to motivate quantum amplification. Independent groups explored microwave masers and optical analogues.
record.pressure: Microwave/radio sources could not provide arbitrarily coherent, narrow, high-frequency radiation. Stimulated emission suggested amplification was possible, but population inversion, resonator design and extension from microwave to optical frequencies were unresolved engineering/physics problems.
rivalsAndFailures: Multiple teams developed overlapping maser/laser concepts, making single-inventor priority an incomplete causal account.
The first ruby laser was pulsed and not automatically optimal for communications or precision frequency applications; gas and later semiconductor lasers occupied different regimes.
An elegant optical-maser proposal still required suitable gain media, pumping and low-loss resonators before physical closure.
record.secondOrderEffects: Coherent light drastically expanded experimental precision and enabled new classes of measurement, spectroscopy, communication and later manufacturing.
record.sourceNativeSummary: The maser/laser trajectory is parallel convergence plus instrumentation leverage: the same broad stimulated-emission principle produced multiple device regimes, and the largest consequence was a new controllable observation/action channel rather than victory of one architecture.
record.standardsAndInstitutions: Bell Labs, Columbia, Lebedev/USSR institutes, Hughes Research Labs, universities, patent/prize systems and optical-component industries contributed different theoretical/device pieces.
record.technicalOrScientificTransition: Quantum electronics moved from a microwave proof to a family of coherent sources spanning optical frequencies; the important transition was a new controllable observation/action capability, not one final laser design.
record.title: Maser/laser from parallel quantum-electronics theory to first working lasers and new measurement capability

candidateRoutes: retain navigational databases
relational model plus high-level query language
relational prototype without aggressive optimization
commercial relational systems
special-purpose file/index systems
decisiveTests: answer useful workloads without exposing record navigation
optimizer-selected plans compete with expert hand-crafted paths
concurrency/recovery/storage make the model operational
record.diffusionAndScaling: Diffusion depended on complements, cost/yield/standards and institutional adoption; the nominal breakthrough date did not equal broad effective use.
record.externalitiesAndCorrections: Lifecycle harms and authority changes are preserved where evidenced rather than inferred from local technical success.
observationsAndInstruments: Codd formalized relations and data independence in 1970.
IBM System R tested the model as an industrial prototype.
SQL exposed set-oriented queries above storage paths.
Cost-based optimization translated declarative queries into physical plans.
record.preExistingWorldModel: Hierarchical/network databases worked and were optimized around known access paths. Codd proposed separating logical relations from physical storage, but performance was uncertain.
record.pressure: Large databases were hard to query because applications depended on physical record layouts and navigation paths; new questions required specialist programs.
rivalsAndFailures: Conceptual simplicity could require implementation sophistication underneath.
High-level queries did not remove physical layout, indexes or cost estimation.
Early performance skepticism could be rational before prototype closure.
record.secondOrderEffects: A declarative representation became practical only when hidden physical optimization, transactions and storage machinery could honor it at acceptable cost; abstraction and implementation were co-produced.
record.sourceNativeSummary: A declarative representation became practical only when hidden physical optimization, transactions and storage machinery could honor it at acceptable cost; abstraction and implementation were co-produced.
record.standardsAndInstitutions: Laboratories, firms, standard bodies, regulators, users and infrastructure operators owned different parts of evidence, implementation and consequence.
record.technicalOrScientificTransition: A declarative representation became practical only when hidden physical optimization, transactions and storage machinery could honor it at acceptable cost; abstraction and implementation were co-produced.
record.title: Relational databases from Codd model through System R, SQL and cost-based optimization

candidateRoutes: replace all networks with one universal network
application-specific gateways
end-to-end internetwork protocol over heterogeneous networks
formal layered standards
proprietary vendor networking
decisiveTests: route across multiple packet technologies without assuming one link behavior
survive loss/reordering with end-to-end semantics
coordinate host conversion and addressing/naming
record.diffusionAndScaling: Diffusion depended on complements, cost/yield/standards and institutional adoption; the nominal breakthrough date did not equal broad effective use.
record.externalitiesAndCorrections: Lifecycle harms and authority changes are preserved where evidenced rather than inferred from local technical success.
observationsAndInstruments: Cerf/Kahn work separated internetworking from any single underlying network.
TCP experimentation led to separation of IP datagrams from end-to-end transport.
Demonstrations linked packet radio, satellite and ARPANET.
BSD distributed TCP/IP implementations.
The 1 January 1983 conversion moved operational ARPANET hosts from NCP to TCP/IP.
record.preExistingWorldModel: ARPANET NCP worked inside one network, while radio/satellite/local networks had different packet sizes, loss, delay and administration.
record.pressure: Packet networks existed but used incompatible host/network assumptions; communication had to work across independently administered heterogeneous networks.
rivalsAndFailures: NCP was useful inside ARPANET but insufficient for internetworking.
A strong protocol without deployable host software and transition operations would not create an Internet.
Later OSI competition showed formal international standardization alone did not guarantee deployment.
record.secondOrderEffects: The Internet emerged from an architecture tolerant of heterogeneous local networks plus a long operational transition of implementations, addressing, naming and institutions.
record.sourceNativeSummary: The Internet emerged from an architecture tolerant of heterogeneous local networks plus a long operational transition of implementations, addressing, naming and institutions.
record.standardsAndInstitutions: Laboratories, firms, standard bodies, regulators, users and infrastructure operators owned different parts of evidence, implementation and consequence.
record.technicalOrScientificTransition: The Internet emerged from an architecture tolerant of heterogeneous local networks plus a long operational transition of implementations, addressing, naming and institutions.
record.title: TCP/IP internetworking from heterogeneous packet networks to the 1983 operational transition

record.sourceNativeSummary: OSI protocol stack: broad international standardization that lost deployment to TCP/IP is retained as a failure/parallel/delayed trajectory because its outcome depended on a sequence of evidence, complements, institutions and lifecycle constraints rather than a single invention date.
record.title: OSI protocol stack: broad international standardization that lost deployment to TCP/IP

candidateRoutes: continue incremental Sanger-pipeline scaling
develop radically cheaper sequencing technologies
convert reference sequencing infrastructure into population-scale reusable data resources
decisiveTests: sequence accuracy and coverage at HGP completion
cost per genome and sequencing throughput over time
ability of new platforms to support population-scale sequencing and rapid public data release
record.diffusionAndScaling: The scientific value expanded through cheaper sequencing and shared reference/variation resources rather than by repeating the original HGP organizational form.
record.externalitiesAndCorrections: Privacy, consent and interpretation remained separate constraints from raw sequencing capability.
observationsAndInstruments: The HGP announced completion in April 2003 after a draft-to-finished production phase.
NHGRI estimated a hypothetical second high-quality reference genome at roughly tens of millions of dollars in 2003, while tracking continuing cost decline.
NHGRI launched the $1,000 Genome technology programme in 2004 to pursue orders-of-magnitude cost reduction rather than treating HGP completion as the end state.
The 1000 Genomes Project later exploited new sequencing platforms and public data release to move from one reference toward population variation.
record.preExistingWorldModel: The Human Genome Project had scaled clone-based mapping and Sanger sequencing into a coordinated international production effort; sequence maps, public databases and large sequencing centers already existed.
record.pressure: Finishing a first human reference sequence made genome-wide biology possible but did not make routine individual-genome sequencing economically or operationally tractable.
rivalsAndFailures: HGP completion did not itself solve affordable individual sequencing.
Continued incremental sequencing improvements competed with explicit investment in high-risk new technology.
record.secondOrderEffects: Cheaper sequencing enlarged the feasible study population and shifted bottlenecks toward data interpretation, study design and clinical validity.
record.sourceNativeSummary: A completed reference sequence became a platform only because sequencing technology, cost curves, shared data, institutional programmes and population resources continued to evolve after 2003.
record.standardsAndInstitutions: International consortia, NHGRI funding, public-data release norms and database operators jointly sustained the transition.
record.technicalOrScientificTransition: The trajectory moved from a one-off international reference-construction programme toward a reusable sequencing/data production capability whose cost, throughput and public-data interfaces became first-class scientific infrastructure.
record.title: Human Genome reference completion to sequencing-platform and cost transition

candidateRoutes: study CRISPR as bacterial adaptive immunity
reconstitute Cas9 cleavage biochemically
engineer guide RNA to redirect cleavage
test whether the mechanism transfers into eukaryotic cells
decisiveTests: does Cas9 cut only when the required RNA components and matching target are present
can guide sequence changes redirect cleavage to predetermined DNA sites
does the mechanism function in eukaryotic-cell genome editing
record.diffusionAndScaling: After the programmable-cleavage result, multiple laboratories rapidly transferred the operation across organisms and cell systems.
record.externalitiesAndCorrections: Precision at a target site does not by itself settle off-target, delivery, germline or governance questions.
observationsAndInstruments: Genetic and microbiological work established CRISPR-Cas as adaptive immunity.
The 2012 Jinek et al. study reconstituted tracrRNA/crRNA-directed Cas9 cleavage and engineered a single guide RNA for sequence-specific DNA cutting.
Multiple groups soon demonstrated genome modification in mouse and human cells.
record.preExistingWorldModel: CRISPR loci and Cas proteins were known, but their immune function and the mechanism by which Cas9 could be directed to DNA were progressively resolved.
record.pressure: Researchers were trying to understand an unusual bacterial repeat/Cas system and its role in host-virus interaction; no programmable genome-editing platform was the original objective.
rivalsAndFailures: Cas9 alone did not cut target DNA in early reconstruction attempts without the required RNA components.
A bacterial mechanism did not automatically establish safe or effective therapeutic editing.
record.secondOrderEffects: The work turned a biological mechanism into a general experimental platform, substantially lowering the cost of targeted genome manipulation.
record.sourceNativeSummary: CRISPR-Cas9 was not born as a generic editing product: understanding a bacterial immune mechanism, discovering required RNA components, reconstructing cleavage and then testing programmability created the transferable operation.
record.standardsAndInstitutions: Universities, journals, shared sequence knowledge and later regulatory institutions governed different phases of discovery and use.
record.technicalOrScientificTransition: A source-native immune mechanism became a programmable molecular operation only after mechanism isolation, biochemical reconstruction and transfer tests.
record.title: CRISPR from adaptive bacterial immunity to programmable genome editing

record.sourceNativeSummary: Modified-mRNA platform before pandemic-scale payoff is retained as a bounded historical trajectory with chronology/outcome boundary locked before any frozen-theory or prior-residual mapping. The control contract does not claim Deep-Anchor causal completeness.
record.title: Modified-mRNA platform before pandemic-scale payoff

record.sourceNativeSummary: Early mRNA vaccination concepts faced inflammatory response, inefficient expression and delivery constraints; the 2005 modified-nucleoside result removed one mechanistic barrier, but platform realization still required delivery, antigen design, trials, manufacturing and exceptional institutional investment.
record.title: mRNA vaccine platform from modified nucleosides to pandemic-scale realization

record.sourceNativeSummary: Predicting 3D protein structure from amino-acid sequence had remained difficult for decades. AlphaFold2 produced a major 2020 breakthrough and later prediction resources expanded access from a benchmark result to a reusable scientific substrate.
record.title: AlphaFold2 from protein-structure prediction bottleneck to database-scale predicted structures

record.sourceNativeSummary: Decades of interferometer, isolation, laser, control, waveform-model and distributed-detector development culminated in the September 2015 GW150914 observation, the first direct gravitational-wave detection.
record.title: LIGO direct gravitational-wave detection to a new observational channel

record.sourceNativeSummary: After decades of experiments and repeated near-misses, NIF achieved target ignition/energy gain on December 5 2022 with 2.05 MJ laser energy delivered to the target and 3.15 MJ fusion output; later shots repeated ignition with higher yield.
record.title: National Ignition Facility fusion ignition and the realization gap to energy systems
